title: One-way functions from hardness of learning P/poly
formal: Does worst-case computational hardness of distribution-free PAC learning of polynomial-size Boolean circuits from random labeled examples imply the existence of one-way functions? Precisely, let \(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) be the size-parameterized uniform learning assertion below, and let \(\mathsf{OWF}\) mean the existence of an ordinary uniformly computable one-way function secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter. The target is \[\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{OWF}.\] Equivalently, would the nonexistence of all such one-way functions guarantee an efficient learner for every target circuit and every example distribution? Hardness here is the failure of efficient learning in the worst case over targets and distributions; no efficiently samplable distribution of hard target descriptions, depth promise on those descriptions, or hardness reduction from SAT is assumed.

source_formulation.text: Does worst-case hardness of efficiently learning polynomial-size circuits from random examples imply the existence of one-way functions?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: One-way functions provide the basic computational ingredient for much of classical private-key cryptography. The question asks whether failure of a general-purpose circuit learner is already enough to supply that ingredient, without assuming that hard target functions can be efficiently generated at random.
status_note: Explicitly open in the checked 2021 conference and full manuscript. Later checked results do not match the unrestricted implication: FOCS 2023 has samplable-average or computational-depth-dependent guarantees; ITCS 2025 Theorem 6 imposes computational shallowness and a particular infinitely-often learning convention; STOC 2026 Theorem 1.5 concerns average-case GapLearn and infinitely-often one-way functions. The 2025 journal metadata/abstract were checked, but subscription full text was unavailable. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution, so current status remains uncertain. Ordinary uniform strong OWF security and all learning parameters are explicit in the formulation.

progress.text: The conference paper states the worst-case-learning-to-OWF question in footnote 6, alongside the stronger-class robustness results and known average-case connections.
The full ECCC manuscript retains the same question in footnote 5.
Hirahara–Nanashima give universal learning results with average-case hidden advice and depth-dependent worst-case running time, and explicitly distinguish security and learning-length quantifiers.
Liu–Mazor–Pass characterize ordinary one-way functions by hardness of black-box learning with a computational-shallowness promise and the stated infinitely-often learning convention.
Hirahara–Nanashima sharpen the average-case description-approximation characterization of Pessiland; their GapLearn theorem includes infinitely-often one-way functions.

Checked source definitions and later theorem promises, including target size, uniformity, input-length frequency and sampler access. No checked result resolves the unrestricted implication; current status is recorded as uncertain.

importance.reason: A broad bridge between worst-case computational learning and the existence of basic cryptographic hardness. The distinction between arbitrary hard targets and efficiently generated hard distributions, as well as the security-length quantifiers, is foundational rather than a parameter improvement.

sentences: The card asks whether failure of efficient worst-case circuit learning already implies ordinary one-way functions.
The learner receives independent noiseless examples under any input distribution and must output a small ordinary Boolean predictor.
A one-way function is uniformly easy to evaluate but has negligible inversion probability for every efficient uniform adversary at all sufficiently large lengths.
Known reverse connections impose efficiently sampled targets, low computational depth, different learning-length quantifiers or a different description-approximation problem.
The completed card preserves the unrestricted implication and records those distinctions while leaving its current status uncertain.

definitions:
Fix ordinary acyclic one-output Boolean circuits with two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants, together with a standard effective binary encoding. For integers \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), let \(\mathcal C(n,s)\) be all functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by such a circuit with at most \(s\) input nodes and gates in total. Polynomial-size circuit families, with no uniform construction requirement across lengths, form \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). The public bound \(s\) exposes the source’s usual polynomial-in-target-size learning convention; the hidden target description is not an input to the learner.

\(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) means that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for all \(n,s\) as above, all integers \(a,b\ge3\), all \(f\in\mathcal C(n,s)\), and all probability distributions \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), the following holds. Given \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim D\), the machine runs for at most \(p(n+s+a+b)\) steps on every execution and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) with \[\Pr_{A,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer randomness consists of the training draws and independent fair machine coins; the inner draw is fresh. Example requests, reading their bits, all computation and output bits count toward the bound. The hypothesis may have size larger than \(s\), but its description and evaluation remain polynomially bounded by the learning time. It needs no further samples or access to \(f\) when evaluated. It is not required to reconstruct the target circuit, identify a unique representation, or be a member of the size-\(s\) class. This avoids imposing proper learning at the prescribed size. The learner has no membership queries, equivalence queries, nonuniform advice or code for sampling \(D\). The example source supplies independent draws even for distributions with no short sampling program. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed target. Arbitrarily large inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters \(a,b\) express ordinary PAC accuracy/confidence. Worst-case hardness is the logical negation of this uniform guarantee, not a lower bound against one particular learner or one restricted type of output.

\(\mathsf{OWF}\) means that there exist a polynomial-time computable length function \(\ell\) and one deterministic polynomial-time machine \(F\) giving maps \(F_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}\), such that for every uniform randomized polynomial-time machine \(I\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), there is \(N_{I,k}\) for which, for all \(n\ge N_{I,k}\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}\big[I(1^n,F_n(x))\in\{0,1\}^n\ \land\ F_n(I(1^n,F_n(x)))=F_n(x)\big]\le n^{-k}.\] In this display the inverter is run once and its returned string is reused in both tests. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on \(n\)-bit strings, independent of inverter coins. Equivalently the event says that the one returned string is any length-\(n\) preimage of \(F_n(x)\), not necessarily \(x\) itself. Invalid output is failure. Evaluation of the family is uniform in \(n\), with no secret key, trapdoor or advice; \(1^n\) tells the inverter the input length. Its running time is polynomial in \(n\). The probability bound is negligible: it is eventually below every inverse power. This is the ordinary all-sufficiently-large-lengths strong one-way notion, not only security on infinitely many lengths. These uniformity and length conventions are made explicit because later learning characterizations use several different variants. No efficient transformation with a specified runtime overhead between witnesses is additionally requested; the target is the existential implication itself.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation \(\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\land\neg\mathsf{OWF}\). A positive result must derive a single uniform one-way family with negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths from the stated unrestricted worst-case learning failure. It may equivalently prove a distribution-free learner from nonexistence of such families, but the learner must handle every target and distribution, not merely a samplable average or a special low-description-complexity promise. A result giving only an auxiliary-input primitive or infinitely-often security is a different conclusion unless its upgrade to the stated notion is proved. An oracle-relative separation or a limitation on a specified reduction method alone does not refute the ordinary implication. This is an existence question with exact logical quantifiers, not a numerical approximation problem.

context_blocks.text: The forward evaluation of a hidden target circuit is easy when its description is known. Learning is different: from observed input-output examples the learner must build a predictor that works on future draws. The challenge is computational, since a polynomial-size description and enough noiseless examples already give a finite statistical learning problem.

One-way functions are known to yield pseudorandom functions and thereby hard circuit-learning tasks. The reverse direction in this card starts with only failure of a worst-case learner. The source contrasts that question with classical equivalences based on average-case learning hardness, where an efficient process chooses the hidden target from a distribution.

The source proves a worst-case/average-case robustness theorem for learning the stronger concept classes EXP/poly and PSPACE/poly. The corresponding decision-complexity consequences concern those stronger classes. They do not establish that every worst-case obstruction for ordinary polynomial-size circuits contains cryptographic average-case hardness.

FOCS 2023 Hirahara–Nanashima extends learning under nonexistence of one-way functions to richer agnostic and distribution-learning models. Its average-case guarantees sample the hidden advice or target distribution. Its worst-case guarantees have runtime exponential in the computational depth of the hidden description, where depth compares a time-bounded shortest description with an unbounded shortest description. That depth need not be logarithmic for arbitrary target descriptions.

ITCS 2025 Liu–Mazor–Pass Theorem 6 gives a worst-case characterization using black-box PAC learning under an explicit computational-shallowness promise on the joint sampler and predictor description. It also uses failure of infinitely-often polynomial-time learning for ordinary one-way functions. The theorem is stronger than an average-case-only analogy, but its promise and length quantifiers do not supply the unrestricted antecedent of this card.

STOC 2026 Hirahara–Nanashima studies approximation of the minimum program description needed for agnostic learning. Its Theorem 1.5 connects average-case hardness of the GapLearn decision problem to infinitely-often one-way functions, with an approximation factor governed by advice complexity of sampling. A minimum-description decision problem, average-case input choice and infinitely-often security are each distinct from this card’s exact implication.

The 2021 full source expressly retains the question. The 2025 journal version’s metadata and abstract were checked, but its subscription full text was not available. The checked 2023–2026 theorems clarify important partial connections without a matching resolution; the card therefore records uncertain current status rather than treating a bounded literature search as proof of openness.
